paper_title: PINT: A Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generalist robot manipulation can benefit from pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning and video generation models (VGMs) for world modeling. However, existing unified models that directly fuse them through shared attention at multiple layers can make it harder to draw on their specialized capabilities. We introduce PINT, a unified model that coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through a shared chunk-level Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. PINT inserts learnable Intent Tokens into the VLM sequence to form this representation, conditioning both the VGM and an Action Expert (AE). It replaces only the VGM's prompt conditioning and retains the VGM at inference, where the AE reads its representations through one-way attention. Rather than prescribing what Predictive Intent should encode, PINT learns it jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE, which provide complementary views of the same upcoming task execution. Training uses two stages: Stage 1 freezes the VGM so that future video prediction shapes Predictive Intent with task-relevant future dynamics, while Stage 2 fixes the learned Intent and adapts the VGM and AE. Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves strong in-distribution (ID) performance and substantially improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, reaching 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard compared with 1.8% for Fast-WAM and 3.2% for StarVLA, and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus compared with 51.5% and 75.0%, respectively. Across five real-world bimanual tasks, PINT reaches 68% ID and 24% OOD success, compared with 35%/9% for pretrained Motus and 67%/35% for pretrained $π_{0.5}$.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Generalist robot manipulation requires understanding and interacting with complex physical environments across diverse tasks. Leveraging the semantic knowledge and reasoning capabilities of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), VisionLanguage-Action (VLA) models translate visual and linguistic understanding into robot actions [3, 4, 5]. Yet standard VLAs do not explicitly model future physical dynamics. In parallel, large-scale video pretraining equips video generation models (VGMs) with strong priors over physical dynamics [6]. Recent World-Action Models (WAMs) [7, 8] leverage these priors for future video prediction and action generation, but typically do not exploit the semantic reasoning of VLMs. Together, these advances motivate unified models that integrate semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation. This raises central challenge: how to effectively combine the complementary capabilities of pretrained VLMs and VGMs. Recent unified models often directly fuse vision-language, video, and action representations through shared attention at multiple layers [1, 9]. Yet pretrained VLMs and VGMs acquire their capabilities through different architectures, conditioning schemes, and learning objectives. These differences lead to specialized internal representations. Direct fusion forces these representations to serve both expert-specific computation and cross-expert coordination, which can make it harder to draw on each pretrained experts specialized capabilities. Several methods instead preserve selected pretrained components or introduce structured interaction pathways [10, 11]. These approaches highlight core tension between expert integration and specialization. The key question is what to share for coordination and what to preserve for specialization. To this end, we propose PINT  (Fig. 1)  , unified model that coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through shared Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. Predictive Intent is compact, chunk-level representation of the upcoming task execution. PINT inserts learnable Intent Tokens into the VLM sequence to form this representation, which conditions both the VGM and the Action Expert (AE). PINT replaces only the VGMs prompt conditioning, preserving its pretrained generative pathway, and retains the VGM at inference, where the AE reads its representations through one-way attention. Rather than prescribing what Predictive Intent should encode, PINT learns it jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE, which provide complementary views of the same upcoming task execution. To facilitate learning of Predictive Intent, PINT adopts two-stage training strategy: Stage 1 freezes the VGM, forcing future video optimization to rely on the Predictive Intent and shaping it with task-relevant future dynamics. Stage 2 then freezes the VLM and Intent Tokens while adapting the VGM and AE to refine video and action generation. We compare PINT with representative VLA, WAM, and unified models, including Motus [1] as representative of direct fusion, across simulation and real-world settings. Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves strong in-distribution (ID) performance and substantially improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. On RoboTwin 2.0-Hard [12], PINT reaches 15.5% success, compared with 1.8% for Fast-WAM [8] and 3.2% for StarVLA [13]. On LIBERO-Plus [14], PINT reaches 79.5% success, compared with 51.5% for Fast-WAM and 75.0% for StarVLA. Across five real-world bimanual tasks, PINT reaches 68% ID and 24% OOD success, compared with 35%/9% for pretrained Motus [1] and 67%/35% for pretrained π0.5 [2]. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce Predictive Intent, compact chunk-level representation that serves as shared interface across specialized experts. It is learned jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE without prescribing what it should encode. 2 PINT: Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation We propose PINT, which realizes Predictive Intent through learnable Intent Tokens that condition both the VGM and AE, and replaces only the VGMs prompt conditioning, preserving its pretrained generative pathway. The VGM remains active at inference so that the AE can draw on its representations through one-way attention, while two-stage strategy lets future video supervision shape Predictive Intent with the VGM frozen before adapting the VGM and AE. Across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world bimanual manipulation, PINT achieves strong ID performance and substantially improves OOD generalization without embodied pretraining. It outperforms comparable VLA and WAM baselines under OOD evaluation, matches pretrained π0.5 on real-world ID tasks, and outperforms pretrained Motus under both ID and OOD evaluation.

sections.title: 2.1 Vision-Language-Action and World-Action Models
sections.content: VLA models adapt pretrained VLMs for robot action generation. RT-2 transfers web-scale vision-language knowledge to robotic control through action tokenization [3], while OpenVLA scales this paradigm to diverse robot demonstrations [4]. Later work improves continuous action generation with π0 [5], action tokenization with FAST [15], and open-world generalization with π0.5 [2]. Recent extensions further improve downstream adaptation, temporal memory, and contact-rich manipulation [16, 17, 18]. Several VLA approaches introduce explicit future supervision, including future image goals in CoT-VLA, future prediction in UP-VLA, and world knowledge forecasting in DreamVLA [19, 20, 21]. complementary line more directly couples future visual prediction with action generation. GR-1 and GR-2 jointly model future visual observations and robot actions, leveraging large-scale video generative pretraining for manipulation [22, 23]. Recent WAMs extend this direction through unified image and action generation in WorldVLA [24], pretrained video diffusion in DreamZero [7], and training-time video modeling without future denoising at inference in Fast-WAM [8].

sections.title: 2.2 Unified Semantic, World, and Action Modeling
sections.content: Recent unified policies combine semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through shared or interacting model components. Representative approaches couple these capabilities through multi-expert interaction, shared video and action representations, or unified generative backbones, including Motus, MotuBrain, LingBot-VA, LingBot-VA 2.0, and Cosmos 3 [1, 9, 25, 26, 27]. In these designs, intermediate representations directly mediate information exchange across capabilities. complementary line routes future information through compact representations. World Tokens maps VLM features into tokens that condition both video prediction and action generation [11], while InternVLA-A1.5 learns foresight tokens in an auxiliary expert that shares attention layers with the VLM and replaces the text conditioning of frozen pretrained VGM [10]. Both remove the video branch at inference [11, 10]. WLA-0 conditions its world expert with meta-queries [28], DIAL defines intent as latent visual foresight [29], and LAWA represents future intention through compact latent actions [30]. Other methods represent future evolution through latent queries, visual subgoals, or structured world representations [31, 32, 33, 34]. Compared with World Tokens and InternVLA-A1.5, PINT forms Predictive Intent directly within the VLM sequence, without an external adapter or an auxiliary expert sharing attention with the VLM [11, 10]. PINT first learns Predictive Intent with the VGM frozen, then fixes the learned Intent and adapts the VGM, which remains active at inference and provides representations to the AE through one-way attention.

We use Qwen3.5-4B [42] and Wan2.2-5B [6] as the VLM and VGM backbones. PINT conditions the AE on layer-wise current-frame VGM features, while PINT-VA extends conditioning to all video latents and synchronously denoises future video and action latents at inference. PINT therefore incurs only moderate additional latency over Fast-WAM, while PINT-VA trades substantially higher inference cost for stronger performance. Additional implementation, evaluation, and latency details are provided in Appendices A, B, and D.3. Benchmarks and evaluation. We evaluate PINT on LIBERO [50], LIBERO-Plus [14], RoboTwin 2.0 [12], and five realworld manipulation tasks. For LIBERO, we jointly train on the four standard suites, evaluate on LIBERO for ID performance, and directly transfer the same policy to LIBERO-Plus for OOD evaluation. For RoboTwin 2.0, we train on all 50 tasks using the official clean demonstrations and evaluate Easy and Hard as ID and OOD settings, respectively. For real-world experiments, we evaluate ID and OOD conditions, with OOD jointly varying lighting, background, and object location. Baselines. We compare PINT with representative VLA, WAM, and unified-model baselines. Embodied pretraining provides additional robot experience and can improve downstream performance and generalization, particularly under distribution shift [2, 45]. We therefore group methods by embodied pretraining. Methods without embodied pretraining serve as our primary comparison, while embodied-pretrained methods provide strong references. We highlight Fast-WAM [8], StarVLA [13], and Motus [1] as representative baselines for WAMs, VLAs, and unified models with direct fusion, respectively. sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. As shown in Table 1, PINT achieves 98.0% average success on LIBERO and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus without embodied pretraining. On LIBERO-Plus, PINT substantially outperforms Fast-WAM (51.5%) and surpasses StarVLA-OFT (75.0%) and ResVLA (75.3%), the strongest baseline without embodied pretraining. It also exceeds several embodied-pretrained methods, including Motus (76.0%) and MemoryVLA++ (73.1%). PINT-VA further improves the averages to 98.2% on LIBERO and 81.0% on LIBERO-Plus. RoboTwin 2.0. As shown in Table 2, PINT achieves 68.6% success on Easy and 15.5% on Hard without embodied pretraining. Compared with Fast-WAM, PINT is slightly lower on Easy (68.6% vs. 72.4%) but achieves substantially higher Hard success (15.5% vs. 1.8%), resulting in higher average success rate (42.1% vs. 37.1%). PINT also surpasses Evo-1 (12.5%), the strongest baseline without embodied pretraining on Hard, and exceeds its 39.1% average success rate. PINT-VA further improves Easy, Hard, and average success to 71.9%, 18.1%, and 45.0%, respectively (repeated evaluations and per-task results in Appendices D.2 and D.4). Real-world experiments. Table 3 summarizes five real-world tasks (setup and rollouts in Appendices B.3 and E.3). Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves 68% ID success, matching pretrained π0.5 (67%) and substantially outperforming pretrained Motus (35%). Under OOD evaluation, PINT reaches 24%, outperforming Motus (9%) while remaining below π0.5 (35%).

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced PINT, which coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through shared chunk-level Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. PINT learns this Intent from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE through two-stage strategy that first shapes it with frozen pretrained VGM and then adapts the VGM and AE. Across simulation and real-world manipulation, PINT achieves strong ID performance and improved OOD generalization without embodied pretraining. These results suggest that compact shared predictive interface can coordinate specialized pretrained models for robot manipulation. Limitations. Our evaluation focuses on robot manipulation and single pairing of VLM and VGM backbones. Combining PINT with embodied pretraining and extending it to broader embodied settings and larger-scale training remain future work.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: A.1 Model Configuration and Inference Model components. We instantiate the VLM with Qwen3.5-4B and the VGM with Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, including its pretrained video DiT and VAE. The AE is state-conditioned action DiT based on the ActionDiT architecture of Fast-WAM, with 30 Transformer layers and hidden dimension of 1024. It operates on continuous action chunks and predicts the corresponding flow velocity. Across all benchmarks, PINT uses = 32 Intent Tokens with VLM hidden dimension of 2560. Two independent linear projections with bias map the same Predictive Intent to the conditioning spaces of the VGM and AE: No additional MLP or normalization layer is applied in either projection. PVGM : R2560 R3072, PAE : R2560 R1024. Input organization. The VLM receives each camera view as an independent image, together with the task instruction and the current robot state discretized as text. The 32 Intent Tokens are appended to the multimodal prefix, followed by the training-only autoregressive action suffix. At inference, the autoregressive suffix is omitted. PINT therefore extracts Predictive Intent with single VLM prefix forward pass and does not autoregressively generate action tokens or intermediate reasoning traces. The VGM uses different visual organization from the VLM. Rather than processing the camera views independently, it receives composed multi-view frame. Table 5 summarizes the benchmark-specific visual layouts and state/action dimensions. All VLM views are independently letterboxed to 224 224 before being passed to the VLM. For RoboTwin 2.0 and the real-world ALOHA setup, the head-camera image is resized to 256 320, while each wrist-camera image is resized to 128 160. The head view is placed above the two wrist views, producing 384 320 VGM input. For LIBERO, the 224 224 main and wrist views are placed side by side, producing 224 448 VGM input. Table 5. Benchmark-specific input configuration. Image sizes are reported as height width. The VLM receives camera views independently, whereas the VGM operates on composed multi-view frame. Benchmark Camera views VGM composition State dim. Action dim. RoboTwin 2.0 LIBERO Head + left wrist + right wrist Main + wrist Real-world ALOHA Head + left wrist + right wrist Head above two wrist views, 384 320 Main and wrist views side by side, 224 448 Same layout as RoboTwin 2.0, 384 320 14 8 14 7 14 Video and action configuration. For future video prediction, all benchmarks use nine frames sampled at t, + 4, + 8, . . . , + 32, comprising the current frame and eight future frames over 32 original data steps. We report this horizon in data steps rather than seconds because the underlying control frequency differs across datasets. The AE predicts continuous action chunk of Ha = 32 steps for all benchmarks. The current proprioceptive state is encoded by two-layer MLP with SiLU activation into single 1024-dimensional state token, which is prepended to the 32 action tokens during AE computation and removed before action prediction. The AE receives VGM representations through layer-wise one-way attention. Both the AE and VGM contain 30 Transformer layers. At AE layer ℓ, the action queries attend to the K/V representations produced by VGM layer ℓ, in addition to the AEs own K/V representations. Thus, the AE accesses VGM features throughout the network rather than only from the final VGM layer. 15 PINT: Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation Inference. Default PINT first performs VLM forward pass to obtain Predictive Intent. The composed current frame is then encoded by the pretrained video VAE, and the VGM performs single forward pass conditioned on Predictive Intent. The resulting layer-wise current-frame K/V representations are cached and reused throughout action generation. The AE generates the 32-step action chunk using 10 explicit-Euler denoising steps with the shifted flow-time schedule used in our implementation (shift = 5), after which the predicted actions are mapped back to the original action space. Default PINT does not denoise future-video latents at inference. PINT-VA uses the same model components and keeps Stage 1 unchanged. During Stage 2 and inference, the AE additionally accesses layer-wise VGM features from all video latents. The nine-frame video sequence is temporally compressed by the Wan VAE into three latent time positions, consisting of one current-frame position and two future positions, each with its own spatial latent grid. The current-frame latent remains fixed, while future-video and action latents are synchronously updated using the same 10-step shifted flow-time schedule. Future-video latents are not decoded back to RGB during standard action inference. A.2 Optimization and Hyperparameters Optimization. We use AdamW for all experiments with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, ϵ = 108, and weight decay 0.01. Weight decay is applied to matrix-valued weights, while bias, normalization, and other non-matrix parameters are excluded. Each training stage independently uses linear warm-up over the first 5% of optimization followed by cosine learning-rate decay. Gradients are clipped to maximum norm of 1.0. Training uses BF16 precision with DeepSpeed ZeRO-1 on 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, without gradient accumulation. We use the same module-wise learning-rate schedule across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and the real-world ALOHA experiments. Table 6 summarizes the peak and final learning rates for each trainable component. During Stage 1, the VGM DiT and video VAE are frozen, while the VLM, Intent Tokens, AE, and both Intent projectors are optimized. During Stage 2, the VLM, Intent Tokens, and video VAE are frozen, while the VGM DiT, AE, and both Intent projectors are optimized. Table 6. Module-wise learning rates. Each entry reports the peak learning rate final learning rate after cosine decay. We use the same loss weights across all benchmarks. During Stage 1, the autoregressive, video, and action objectives are weighted by λAR = 0.1, λvideo = 0.1, and λaction = 1.0, respectively. Stage 2 does not execute the autoregressive branch and optimizes only the video and action objectives with λvideo = 0.1 and λaction = 1.0. The autoregressive loss is averaged over valid supervised tokens. The action and video objectives are averaged over valid action elements and future-video latent elements, respectively, and use the timestep-dependent weighting of the flow scheduler. The video objective is applied only to future-video latents, excluding the current-frame latent, and padded elements are masked from the corresponding losses. Training budget. Table 7 summarizes the training budget for each benchmark. Stage 1 uses per-GPU batch size of 16, corresponding to global batch size of 128 across 8 GPUs. Stage 2 uses per-GPU batch size of 12 and global batch size of 96. RoboTwin 2.0 and the real-world ALOHA experiments are trained for 5 epochs in each stage, while LIBERO is trained for 10 epochs per stage. Stage 2 is initialized from the final Stage 1 checkpoint. For all reported results, we evaluate the final Stage 2 checkpoint rather than selecting checkpoints according to validation or test performance. PINT-VA follows the same optimization configuration and training budget as PINT. A.3 Two-Stage Training and Variant Details Initialization and stage transition. Stage 1 initializes the VLM from Qwen3.5-4B and the VGM and video VAE from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. Following Fast-WAM, the AE backbone is initialized by copying or interpolating weights from the pretrained Wan DiT, while newly introduced components, including the action encoder, state encoder, and output head, are initialized separately. The two Intent projectors are randomly initialized. The 32 Intent Token embeddings are initialized with the mean of the original Qwen vocabulary embeddings and are subsequently optimized as independent learnable tokens. During Stage 1, the VGM DiT and video VAE are frozen, while the VLM, Intent Tokens, AE, and both Intent projectors are optimized jointly. Stage 2 is initialized from the final Stage 1 checkpoint without reinitializing the AE or projectors. The VLM, Intent Tokens, and video VAE are then frozen, while the VGM DiT, AE, and both Intent projectors remain trainable. The autoregressive branch is not executed during Stage 2. As described in Appendix A.2, the final Stage 2 checkpoint is used for evaluation. Prompt-conditioned VGM. This variant replaces only the conditioning input to the VGM. Instead of Predictive Intent, the VGM receives the task instruction through the original Wan T5 text-conditioning pathway. The AE continues to use Predictive Intent together with proprioceptive state, and the 32 Intent Tokens remain otherwise unchanged. The Intent-to-VGM projector is bypassed for VGM conditioning. All other components follow the same two-stage schedule, training budget, and checkpoint-selection protocol as PINT. Split Intent. This variant replaces the shared Intent group with two expert-specific groups containing 32 VGM Intent Tokens and 32 AE Intent Tokens: multimodal prefix QVGM QAE AR suffix. The VGM and AE read their corresponding token groups through separate projectors. Under the causal VLM mask, the AE-specific Intent Tokens can attend to the preceding VGM-specific group, while the reverse interaction is not permitted. The remaining expert connections and training procedure are unchanged. Loss ablations. For w/o Stage 1 Video Loss, we remove the future-video prediction objective only during Stage 1. Stage 2 restores the standard video and action objectives. This variant therefore isolates the role of video supervision in shaping Predictive Intent during Stage 1 rather than removing video modeling throughout training. For w/o AR Loss, the autoregressive branch and its objective are removed during Stage 1, while the video and continuous-action objectives remain unchanged. Stage 2 is identical to the default PINT configuration. 17 PINT: Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation Expert-interaction ablation. For w/o VGM-to-AE Features, the AE no longer attends to the layer-wise K/V representations of the VGM. It remains conditioned on Predictive Intent and proprioceptive state, while the VGM continues to optimize the future-video objective. The two-stage training schedule is otherwise unchanged. Training-schedule ablations. Stage 1 Only directly evaluates the final Stage 1 checkpoint without performing Stage 2. Inference remains identical to default PINT: the VLM first produces Predictive Intent, the VGM performs single current-frame forward pass to produce cached layer-wise K/V features, and the AE generates the action chunk with 10 denoising steps. Single-Stage Training jointly optimizes the VLM, Intent Tokens, VGM DiT, AE, and both Intent projectors from initialization, while keeping the video VAE frozen. It uses the autoregressive, video, and action objectives throughout training. On RoboTwin 2.0, it is trained for 10 epochs, matching the total 5 + 5 epoch budget of the default two-stage schedule. The VLM and Intent Tokens use learning rate of 105 106, while the VGM, AE, and both Intent projectors use 104 106. Its inference procedure remains the default current-frame PINT configuration. Intent capacity. The 16and 64-token variants change only the size of the shared Intent group from the default = 32. Both the VGM and AE continue to condition on the full shared group. The projector dimensions remain 2560 3072 for the VGM and 2560 1024 for the AE. All other architectural choices, objectives, optimization settings, and training budgets are kept unchanged. Benchmarks, Data, and Evaluation Fig. 5 summarizes the benchmarks and real-world evaluation settings. B.1 RoboTwin 2.0 RoboTwin 2.0 [12] is bimanual manipulation benchmark built around the Aloha-AgileX dual-arm robot. We jointly train single PINT model on all 50 tasks using 50 official clean demonstrations per task, resulting in 2,500 demonstrations. The tasks cover object interaction, tool use, stacking, handover, lifting, and coordinated dual-arm manipulation. We evaluate the final checkpoint on all 50 tasks under both Easy and Hard. Each evaluation uses 100 rollouts per task and setting with the official simulator success signal. The same checkpoint trained on clean demonstrations is directly evaluated under both settings without additional adaptation. Easy corresponds to the clean ID environment, whereas Hard follows the clean-to-randomized protocol and introduces domain randomization in background appearance, table clutter, lighting, and table height. Table 8 summarizes the configuration differences. B.2 LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus For LIBERO [50], we jointly train single model on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long using 50 demonstrations per task. These suites respectively evaluate spatial reasoning, object-centric manipulation, goal-conditioned behaviors, and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the final checkpoint on all four suites, conducting 50 rollouts per task with the official initial states, reset procedure, and success signal. We directly evaluate the same LIBERO-trained checkpoint on LIBERO-Plus [14] without additional training or adaptation. sections.content: We measure inference latency for Fast-WAM, PINT, and PINT-VA under the same hardware and inference configuration. All measurements are performed on single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU using BF16 precision and batch size 1. For each model, we first run 100 inputs for warm-up, followed by three independent timing rounds of 100 inputs each. We report the mean end-to-end latency over the resulting 300 timed runs. The measured latency covers generation of complete 32-step action chunk with 10 action denoising steps, including the VLM forward pass for PINT and PINT-VA. First, Fig. 6 expands the example in Fig. 3 and shows the corresponding closed-loop future-video predictions under ID and OOD conditions for the task of placing the container on the plate. All models receive the same current frame and task instruction and predict future frames at t+8, t+16, t+24, and t+32, which are compared with the corresponding ground-truth frames from the same demonstration. The ID and OOD examples are drawn from clean and randomized demonstrations, respectively, and therefore need not share the same scene layout. 25 PINT: Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation Figure 7. In the ID examples, the VGM trained in Fast-WAM and both PINT stages generally produce predictions close to the ground truth. Under OOD shifts, the VGM trained in Fast-WAM often shows stronger degradation in scene appearance and structure, particularly for Beat Block Hammer and the Blocks Ranking tasks. PINT better preserves the scene layout in these examples, while Stage 2 generally refines the predicted arm and object motion relative to Stage 1. Prediction quality decreases at the longest horizon for all methods, with visible blurring in some t+32 frames. E.2 Predictive Intent Visualization Details The visualization in Fig. 4 is constructed from RoboTwin 2.0 clean training demonstrations. We extract Predictive Intent every 10 data frames and retain samples with complete 32-step future action chunk. For each retained sample, the visualization pairs the Predictive Intent and ground-truth action chunk from the same episode and timestep. For the two-dimensional coordinates, we use the ground-truth continuous action chunk of shape 32 14. Each action dimension is standardized across the retained samples, after which the chunk is flattened, reduced to 50 dimensions with PCA, and projected to two dimensions with t-SNE. Colors are computed independently from Predictive Intent. We take the final-layer hidden states of the 32 Intent Tokens before the expert-specific projections and mean-pool them across tokens. The resulting representation is projected to three PCA dimensions, which are mapped to the RGB channels. Each channel is independently scaled using its 1st and 99th percentiles PINT: Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation before clipping to the valid color range. The Intent representations are extracted from the final Stage 1 checkpoint. Because Stage 2 freezes the VLM and Intent Tokens, the Predictive Intent representation remains fixed during subsequent expert adaptation. The highlighted regions in Fig. 4 are used only for qualitative inspection of the corresponding demonstration segments and do not represent supervised behavior labels or automatically discovered semantic clusters. 28 E.3 Real-World Qualitative Rollouts PINT: Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation We provide qualitative real-world rollouts to complement the quantitative evaluation of PINT.
